ls.lead: One idea, one gesture, one question. Each right answer stamps your passport.

items.alt: Kūro, sitting on a suitcase, catches an envelope carried by a paper plane
items.d: A client abroad can pay you by four routes. None is the best everywhere: compare the delay, the fees and what your bank accepts.

pick.v: The client wires money to your account. They need your IBAN or account number, your bank’s SWIFT/BIC code and an invoice. Ask your bank first how it receives a transfer from abroad, and in which currency it is credited.

An online service collects the money for you and pays it out to your account or card. Check first, on the service’s own site, that it opens accounts for residents of your country and how money is withdrawn.

The platform charges the client, holds the money until delivery, takes its commission and pays you the rest. Simple to start with: read its commission and its withdrawal methods before you accept a job.
The client sends tokens, often a stablecoin, to your address. It is fast and cannot be undone. Legal in some countries, banned in others, Algeria among them (law 25-10): check the law where you live.

items.q: Before you accept a first payment from abroad, what do you check first?
a: How your bank or the service receives the money, and what it costs you
items.ok: Yes. The route first, the price after.

items.alt: Kūro peeks out of a small vault door, in front of a card and three coins
items.d: A multi-currency account holds several currencies side by side and gives you bank details to be paid with. What costs is almost never the opening: it is three fees.

pick.v: The margin taken when one currency becomes another. Compare the rate you are offered with the market rate on the same day: the gap is your real price.
A fixed amount or a percentage on each sending, each receipt or each withdrawal. A small percentage weighs a lot on a large invoice.
Fees at the cash machine, abroad, or beyond a monthly limit. Read the fee table before you travel, not after.

items.listT: Four questions to ask before you open one
list: Does the service accept residents of my country?
In which currencies can I receive?
How do I withdraw, and at what price?
Who holds and protects my money?
items.q: Two services both say “0 fees”. Where do you look?
items.ok: Yes. A rate worse than the market is a fee that does not say its name.

items.alt: Kūro rests a paw on an abacus, beside a calendar and an hourglass
items.d: A rate is not guessed, it is worked out: what you want to keep, plus your costs, divided by the days you really bill.

f.fine: Your reliable income covers your spending: the savings do not move.

src.title: The course’s sources
src.note: Every figure in this course comes from one of these sources. Where a study is small, or a figure is the company’s own, the level says so.

items.d: Gamification borrows a few of a game’s springs for an activity that is not a game: a course, an app, a site. The activity stays the real thing; the game lends it its way of making you want to.

pick.v: “The use of game design elements in non-game contexts”: the definition proposed by Deterding and colleagues in 2011, the one research has used since.
It is not building a whole game, and it is not a coat of paint. If you take the game away and nothing useful is left, it was not gamification.
In 2010 the game designer Margaret Robertson wrote that the right word for what she was seeing was “pointsification”: points and badges put on anything, without the game.

items.q: Which of the three is gamification?
a: A progress bar in an online course
items.ok: Yes. The course is still a course; the bar lends it one of a game’s springs: seeing that you are moving forward.

items.d: A good game does not hold you with its points. It feeds three needs psychology has long described: to feel capable, to feel free, to feel connected. When an activity feeds them, people come back without being pushed.

pick.v: Immediate feedback and steps within reach: you can see yourself improve. That is the need for competence.
You choose your path and your pace. What becomes compulsory stops being a game. That is the need for autonomy.
Playing with others, or belonging to a shared world. That is the need for relatedness.
From Ryan and Deci’s self-determination theory (2000): three psychological needs, competence, autonomy and relatedness. Satisfied, they strengthen motivation; thwarted, they weaken it.

items.q: A progress bar feeds which need first?
items.ok: Yes: it shows the road already covered. It is competence made visible.

items.d: Does it really help people learn? In 2020 Sailer and Homner pooled 38 publications, 40 experiments in all. Their answer: yes, effects that are small but real, and not all equally solid.

pick.v: On what is learned: g = 0.49. It is the study’s most stable result, even when only the most rigorous experiments are kept.
On motivation: g = 0.36. The authors call it less stable than the first.
On what people actually do: g = 0.25, the smallest of the three, and also less stable.

Two wider reviews say it another way. Hamari and colleagues (2014, 24 studies): positive effects that depend greatly on the context and on the people. Koivisto and Hamari (2019, 819 studies): results that lean positive, with a remarkable share of mixed results.

items.q: What should you take from these studies?
a: It helps a little, when it is well designed for its audience
items.ok: Yes: real, modest effects that depend on the context. Nobody serious promises more.

items.d: A game mechanic answers one precise spring. You choose one or two for a goal, not ten for decoration.

pick.v: Nunes and Drèze (2006): a task of eight steps presented as ten steps with two already done is completed more often, and faster. Starting at 2 of 10 commits you more than starting at 0 of 8.
Kivetz and colleagues (2006), in a real café: the closer customers get to the free coffee, the more often they buy. People speed up near the finish line.
On Stack Overflow, Anderson and colleagues (2013) see activity rise as a badge nears, then fall back. A 2020 study adds a caveat: about 20% of users respond.

Duolingo told its shareholders in November 2026 that it runs hundreds of experiments, on notifications and streaks among other things, to bring users back: 64.9 million a day in the third quarter of 2026.
Completing a set of things: that is what this course’s eight stickers do. The mechanic is in front of you.

items.q: Two loyalty cards both ask for eight car washes. Which one is completed more often?
items.ok: Yes. The same effort, but you have already started: that is the endowed progress effect.

items.t: What it does for a brand
items.d: This level is our reading as practitioners, not a study’s result. A game gives a brand three things a logo alone does not: a voice, a world, and a reason to come back.

pick.v: Here, Kūro judges your answers in two words. A brand that reacts to what you do has a character; a brand that recites has none.
The night workshop, the radio, the DOURO·8 console, the seals: it all comes from the same place. You recognise the brand without seeing its logo.
Stamps, seals, stickers: small ends to reach, which give a reason to finish the page and to come back to it.
If the game hides the offer, the price or the contact, it works against the brand. The game serves the message; it does not replace it.

items.q: What does a brand gain first from being playable?
a: A character people recognise and come back to
items.ok: Yes. The rest may follow, but character is what brings people back.

items.d: Four cases, each with its source and its limit. Two figures come from the companies themselves, and a third from a brand campaign: each time, it is said.

pick.v: The Starbucks Rewards programme has 35.8 million active members in the United States, and 59% of the money taken in the chain’s own U.S. stores comes from its members. Figures published by Starbucks for the quarter ended in late June 2026.
Deloitte added game elements to its executive training platform. Harvard Business Review (2013) reports 37% more users returning to it each week. A company figure, with no comparison group.

An online game in which players fold proteins. In 2011 its players produced, in three weeks, a model accurate enough for researchers to determine the structure of an enzyme from a monkey retrovirus. The result was published in Nature Structural & Molecular Biology.

Stockholm, 2010: for three days, drivers who kept to the limit were entered in a lottery. The average speed reported fell from 32 to 25 km/h. A famous case but a fragile one: three days, no control group, and a figure given by the sponsor, Volkswagen.

items.q: Which of these cases rests on a scientific publication?
items.ok: Yes. The others are company or campaign figures: useful, and to be read as such.

items.d: A game can also demotivate, push and trap. Knowing where it breaks is part of the craft.

pick.v: Lepper, Greene and Nisbett (1973): children who already liked an activity showed less interest in it after doing it for a promised reward. Those who got a surprise reward, or none, kept their interest.

Hanus and Fox (2015) followed two classes for sixteen weeks. The one with badges and a leaderboard ended less motivated, less satisfied, and with lower exam scores. A small study, but a warning: a leaderboard is not a gift to everyone.

In November 2012 the analyst firm Gartner forecast that 80% of the gamified applications of the time would miss their business objectives by 2014, mainly because of poor design. It is a forecast, not a measurement.

In 2022 the U.S. consumer protection agency (FTC) published a report on “dark patterns”, interfaces that push people into choices they would not otherwise have made. The same year the maker of Fortnite agreed to pay 245 million dollars to refund unwanted purchases.

items.q: According to Gartner, why were most of these projects going to fail?
a: People do not like to play
items.ok: Yes. It is not the game that fails, it is the game badly thought out for its goal.

items.d: This site plays, and it has given itself rules. Here they are, with the place to check them.

pick.v: The radio, the clips, Kūro: everything waits for your move, and everything stops with one. On a device set to “reduce motion”, nothing moves.
The DOURO·8 calculator looks like a console, but its receipt adds up lines and its total is their exact sum. The game makes the price readable; it does not dress it up.
Seven seals open a drawing. Eight levels give eight stickers. No reward here is traded for your address or for a purchase.
Stamps, seals and stickers stay in your browser. They are sent nowhere; there is no account and no leaderboard.
No streak to keep, no countdown. You can leave and come back: your progress waits for you.

items.q: On this site, what do you get for seven seals?
items.ok: Yes. That is our rule: we reward with something to look at, never with pressure to buy.

src.note: The advice on security, backups, bandwidth and stays comes from these sources; the calculators’ figures are your own. The ANSSI guide dates from 2019 and addresses employees: its habits hold for a freelancer too. Nothing here is legal or tax advice.

items.d: Clients do not fall from the sky: they answer messages. How many should you send? It can be counted. The clients you want, divided by the share of people who reply, then by the share of those who sign.

f.unit: The starting rates are examples, not averages. Note what you send and what comes back for a month, then put in your own.

items.q: You send 40 messages: 4 people reply, 1 signs. You want 3 clients a month. What do you do?
a: Send 120 messages, or improve one of the two rates
Wait for word of mouth to do the rest
items.ok: Yes. One signature per 40 messages, so 120 messages for 3 clients. Or a better message, or a better offer: both rates can be worked on.

items.d: A project price is time counted before you start: your day rate, times the days you estimate, plus a margin for what you did not see coming. The client wants one figure that no longer moves.

f.dep: at the order, if you ask for 40%
f.unit: In whatever currency you type. To find your day rate:

items.q: The project takes three days more than planned, and the scope has not changed. Who pays for those three days?
a: The client: you send an extra invoice
You: that is what the margin is for
items.ok: Yes, if the price was firm. It is the Studio’s rule: “if the work overruns, the difference is on us”. If the scope changes, that is a new quote.

items.d: A signed quote prevents most disputes, because it answers the awkward questions in advance. Here are five lines, with what the Studio writes in its own. These are our terms, not a legal template.

pick.v: What is included, written as a list: the pages, the languages, the functions. What is not on it is not included. Every other line depends on this one.
At the Studio: 40% at the order, on a signed quote, and 60% at delivery, before the site goes live. A deposit shows the project is real on both sides.
At the Studio: two rounds of revisions per stage, design then development, are included; further ones are quoted separately. Without this line, a project never ends.
At the Studio: once the site is paid in full, it belongs to the client, with the code, the design files and the content. Write down the moment the work changes hands.
At the Studio: the firm deadline is set once the project has been scoped together, not before. A deadline promised before the scope is known is a guess.

items.q: The client asks for a third round of revisions on the design. What does the Studio’s quote say?
items.ok: Yes. Two rounds per stage are included; further ones are quoted separately.

items.d: A client six time zones away is not a problem, it is a calendar. What matters is the hours your two working days share: that is where calls go. The rest is done in writing.

f.none: No shared hour between two 9-to-18 days: one of you will have to shift theirs, or everything goes in writing.
f.unit: Two 9-to-18 days, in whole hours. Algeria is on UTC+1 all year, with no summer time; the client’s summer time, if they have one, can move the window by an hour.

items.q: You are on UTC+1, your client on UTC−5. At what time, on your clock, do you offer the call?
items.ok: Yes. 16:00 for you is 10:00 for your client: the hour falls inside both days.

items.d: Your office fits in a bag: anything that breaks, gets lost or cuts out stops you dead. Three precautions: copies of your files, enough bandwidth for your calls, and a second connection.

pick.v: At least three copies of your files, on two devices, with one backup kept somewhere else. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) calls it a popular strategy that can be used in most scenarios: if one copy is compromised, at least one other is intact.

A one-to-one call needs little. Zoom recommends 600 kbps each way for high-quality video, and 1.2 Mbps for 720p; on a group call, 1 Mbps up and 600 kbps down, and at 720p 2.6 Mbps up and 1.8 Mbps down. Google Meet counts up to 1.7 Mbps per participant at 720p, and lowers the definition when bandwidth is short. These are the vendors’ own figures: test your connection before the call, not during it.
The Wi-Fi where you stay can drop on the day of a call. Keep a second way in: your phone’s hotspot. It is also what the NCSC advises instead of an unknown hotspot: use the mobile network.

items.q: Your bag is stolen: the laptop, and the backup drive that was inside it. What was missing?
items.ok: Yes. That is the “1” in 3-2-1: one copy outside the bag, online or with someone you trust.

items.d: On the road, your accounts are worth more than your gear: a laptop can be bought again, a hacked mailbox much less so. Five habits, each recommended by a public cyber security agency.

pick.v: The French agency, ANSSI, advises avoiding networks you do not control whenever possible: hotel, station or café Wi-Fi. The UK’s NCSC agrees: the simplest precaution is not to connect through an unknown hotspot and to use the mobile network instead; a VPN is another option.
The NCSC recommends turning on 2-step verification for your most important accounts: email, banking, social media, online shopping. It keeps criminals out even if they know your password.
A different password for each account, says ANSSI. And a password manager to remember them for you, says the NCSC, which also advises choosing passkeys wherever they are offered.

The NCSC advises that every laptop use encryption that requires a password to boot: BitLocker on Windows, FileVault on macOS. Keep the recovery key somewhere safe. And before you leave, ANSSI advises finding out about the law of the country you are going to, including on encryption.

Three habits from ANSSI’s guide for professionals who travel: lock your session whenever you step away, even for a moment; do not plug in a USB key you were given without having it checked; carry the strict minimum of data.

items.q: At the airport, you need to sign in to an important account. What is safest?
items.ok: Yes. The mobile network rather than a network you do not control: that is the NCSC’s advice, and ANSSI’s.

items.d: A year has 52 weeks, but you bill only part of it: there are holidays, public holidays, illness, and all the work nobody pays for. Count your billed days before you promise yourself an income.

f.unit: Holidays, public holidays and illness go into the weeks without work. The starting billed share is an example: measure your own.

items.q: You work 5 days a week and bill 60% of them. Over one week, that makes…
items.ok: Yes. The other two days are real: prospecting, quotes, paperwork, learning. Your day rate is what pays for them.

items.d: Going to work somewhere else means four files to open before you buy the ticket: the stay, taxes, health, the bank. The answers depend on your nationality, your status and the country. This lesson gives you the questions, not the answers.

pick.v: Every country has its own rules on entry and length of stay. One official example: in the Schengen area, a short stay is usually a maximum of 90 days within any 180-day period, and the European Commission publishes a calculator to check it. To ask the consulate: does this visa allow me to work remotely for clients in another country?

Where do you pay tax if you spend several months elsewhere? It depends on your tax residence, and on the agreements between the two countries. To ask the tax office or an accountant, before leaving: from when am I a resident here, and what must I still declare at home?
To ask your insurer: am I covered outside my country, for how long, and for repatriation? And the consulate: does my visa require insurance?
To check before you go: does my card work abroad, and at what cost? Does my bank send its codes by text message, and will my number receive them there? Who receives my post in the meantime?

items.q: You leave the Schengen area for one day, then come back. The 90-day count…
a: carries on: it looks at the previous 180 days
items.ok: Yes. You count back 180 days from each day of your stay: leaving for a day erases nothing. The Commission’s calculator does the count for you.

For the Design Council, the UK’s design body, “your brand is more than a logo”: first sort what you have.

items.d: “Everyone” is not an audience, and a logo made for everyone speaks to no one. The Design Council puts the target audience in every brief (the document that explains the project to the designer). Describe one person: what they want to get, where they find you, what makes them hesitate.

items.d: “The best quality”: your competitors say it too. A promise says what a client gets from you; a proof makes it believable: a written deadline, a figure to show, a signed review. Here a brief starts there: that is our method, not a rule.

items.ex: For example: “made-to-order cakes ready at the agreed time, or refunded”; “a written quote that does not move, fitting included”. These are examples, not lines to copy.

items.rule: The workshop’s rule: replace every adjective with a fact a client can observe.

items.ok: Yes. A deadline can be checked. “Best” cannot.
no: No. “Best” cannot be observed: no customer can check it.
No. Passion cannot be shown: it takes a fact a customer can observe.

items.d: “I want blue”: and the designer has nothing left to look for. The Design Council advises describing the goal, not the solution. Say what people should feel, with three sliders: the designer chooses the means.

a: “I want blue and a round typeface”
“We should come across as generous and careful, like a table laid for a celebration”
“Do what the competitor did, but better”
items.ok: Yes. The goal, not the means: they find the means.
no: No. That is already the solution: state the goal, the designer chooses the means.
No. Copying a competitor means being mistaken for them: say what people should feel with you.

l: A brand I like, and why (optional)

refs.note: Two are enough, if you say why: the “why” is what the designer uses.

items.d: Your printer asks for the logo for a 3-metre banner, and all you have is a JPEG. An identity is a set of files, and each one has a job. Open them one by one: they are the ones to look for in any proposal.

pick.v: A drawing made of shapes, not dots: for the printer, the sign, the banner. According to the web’s reference documentation (MDN), an SVG vector image renders at any size without loss of quality, unlike a PNG or a JPEG.
An image with no background, to place the logo on a document or a photo. It is a pixel image: we deliver it large enough for screens, and keep the vector for the rest.
Colour, one colour, black, white; long and square. For us, that is what stops the logo being squashed to fit somewhere.

The rule book: sizes, margins, colours, what is not allowed. It lets someone else make a consistent visual without calling you. Complete guidelines also give each colour a role (text, surface, accent, alert) and a reading order (title, details, action): that is our list. The W3C’s accessibility rules (WCAG 2.2) require a minimum contrast between text and its background: ask for a role per colour, and text that stays readable.
A font has a licence. The SIL OFL, a free licence for fonts, allows use in a logo and in print according to its own FAQ. For a paid font, ask who holds the licence and what it covers.

The guide by WIPO (the World Intellectual Property Organization) and INAPI for Algeria (2004) says it: the creator of a logo first holds its copyright; it advises settling this in the initial agreement, or having the right formally assigned to your company. In France, under the Intellectual Property Code, each right transferred must be named in the deed: ask for the assignment in writing.

pick.k: The campaign master and its formats
pick.v: One master file in separate layers (background, subject, text), then the formats cut from it, for example a square, a vertical story, a banner. With us, the master is kept and only what the frame shows changes; one page of rules says what may move and what may not.

items.q: For her second shop, the printer asks Nadia (our example) for the logo for a 3-metre banner. She sends…
a: a phone photo of the logo
the PNG from her social media page

no: No. A photo is made of dots: enlarged to 3 metres, it blurs.
No. A PNG is a pixel image, made for the screen: not for a banner.

items.t: The name, and whose it is
items.d: Your logo is drawn and paid for: it is not yet protected as a trademark. A mark is registered, country by country, with the national office, or through the Madrid System that WIPO runs. Pick a country to see whom to ask and what the official texts say.

pick.v: The office is INAPI; a mark lasts ten years, renewable. According to INPI’s sheet on Algeria (June 2025), INAPI itself examines whether the name is free, and a filer with no domicile in Algeria goes through an agent (someone who files in their name). The fees are on INAPI’s page: check them on the day you file.
pick.more: Also, according to the same sheet: registration takes about two years on average, a mark unused for more than three years is lost, and .dz names are reserved for entities established in Algeria or holders of a mark valid in Algeria.

pick.v: The office is INPI. A mark lasts ten years, renewable without limit, and must be used. INPI’s fee schedule applicable from 2 July 2026: filing €190 for one class (a category of goods or services), €40 per extra class, renewal €290 for one class. INPI’s search for earlier logos (marks already filed that look like yours) costs €532 for one class.

Registration is with the Ministry of Economy and Tourism. Its page lists AED 750 to apply, AED 750 for publication and AED 5,000 for registration, AED 6,500 in all, then 30 days for objections after publication. A foreign owner goes through an agent (someone who files in their name).

WIPO points to each national office, and to the Madrid System for several countries in one application. The question to ask the office: is this name free in my class (my category of goods or services)?

web3c.lead: You were sold a chain; perhaps all you wanted was loyal customers. Two ways to follow this course. You have a project: eight steps to tell the tool from the result, and leave with a brief that can be priced. You want to understand: nine modules, from the foundations to security, with a diagram to work with at every step. Sometimes a chain is the right tool; this course helps you tell when. items.d: You were told about tokens, NFTs, wallets: before the words, your idea. Write it in one sentence, without any of them, then open them one by one. Web3 is a site that talks to a shared ledger instead of a private database.

pick.v: A ledger copied on many machines, where lines are added without rewriting the history. That is how NIST, the US standards agency, describes it.
An app or a device that keeps your keys. It does not hold the tokens: they stay on the network (ethereum.org, a community documentation site).
A line of the ledger that says who owns what: an interchangeable unit, or a unique object. What an NFT holder gets depends on what its creator set up (ethereum.org).

The site reads your public address; it can move nothing without your signature. But a signature can be a spending approval: according to ethereum.org it does not expire, disconnecting does not remove it, you have to revoke it. Connecting, signing a message and signing a transaction are three different requests: step 4 tells them apart.
The private key signs; the phrase recreates it. NIST puts it plainly: lose the key, lose the asset. The European authorities: never share it, whoever has it takes control.

A program published in the ledger. It runs as programmed when a transaction calls it, and its deployed code is public in the ledger. According to ethereum.org, once deployed it usually cannot be patched.
A token designed to track a currency. The European authorities warn it may not stay so stable, especially when markets are under stress.
Every action pays the network, and the amount moves with demand. According to ethereum.org, the fee is paid whether the transaction succeeds or fails.

The MiCA regulation (the EU regulation on markets in crypto-assets) covers e-money tokens, asset-referenced tokens and other crypto-assets, utility tokens among them; according to the European authorities, NFTs in a series or collection may fall within it. According to ESMA (the European Securities and Markets Authority), providers authorised under MiCA are listed in its register: check the provider there. Whom to ask: the country’s financial regulator.

Since 1 July 2026, according to the AMF (France’s financial markets authority), only crypto-asset service providers authorised under MiCA (PSCA) may serve clients in France; the AMF publishes their white list. An unauthorised provider faces two years in prison and a €30,000 fine. This concerns crypto-asset service providers, not every NFT project: is yours one? A question for the AMF or a lawyer.

VARA (Dubai’s Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority) regulates virtual assets in Dubai, outside the DIFC (the Dubai International Financial Centre). Its 2024 rules: only a VARA-licensed provider, or someone acting for it with approval, may market them; the advert must say they may lose their value in full or in part, and never promise safety or a return.

ch.tabs: The six lessons of the build

items.d: The browser sends a request with a method, an address and headers. The server returns a status and often a body; according to MDN, the web’s reference documentation, statuses fall into five classes, from 100 to 599. The interface translates those results into states a person understands.

pick.v: The request has gone and nothing has come back: a waiting state that does not block the page.
A 200 with an empty list is a success. The screen says “No workshops yet”, not “error”.
A 200 with workshops: the list renders.
A 500, or no answer: a separate message and a way to retry. According to MDN, a 503 means the server is temporarily unavailable.

items.ex: A workshop page requests an event list. A valid empty list should render a helpful empty state. An unexpected server error needs a separate message.
items.try: Draw loading, empty, success and error versions of the event list. Match each version to a network condition.
items.check: An empty 200 response becomes an empty state. A failed request becomes an error state with a way to retry where appropriate.
items.q: The workshop list comes back empty, with a 200 status. The screen shows…
a: a helpful empty state: “No workshops yet”
items.ok: Yes. An empty 200 is a success: say there is nothing, not that it failed.

items.h: Make the data tell the truth.
items.d: Give each entity a stable identifier, link them with foreign keys, and let the database enforce what it can enforce. Keep the display name separate from the identifier. That is our workshop’s method.

pick.v: id · name. A room hosts several workshops.
id · title · capacity · room_id. The title may change, the identifier never.
id · workshop_id · name · state. It points to the workshop’s identifier, not to its title.

items.ex: Workshop records have an ID and a capacity. Booking records reference the workshop ID. A renamed workshop keeps its existing bookings.
items.try: Sketch a schema for a room that hosts several events and an event that accepts many bookings.
items.check: Room, workshop, booking: two one-to-many relationships. The booking stores workshop_id, so it stays attached when the workshop title changes.
items.q: A workshop changes its title. Its bookings…
items.ok: Yes. Link by identifier, never by the display name.

items.d: A contract states the accepted input and the response for each meaningful outcome. Validate on the server and give clients stable error identifiers. Run three possible requests: the server’s response changes the interface.

see: “That workshop is full. See other dates.”
lab.src: According to MDN: 201, the request succeeded and a new resource was created; 400, the server will not process a request perceived as a client error; 409, the request conflicts with the current state of the server.

items.ex: POST /bookings accepts a workshop identifier and a name. A successful creation, malformed input and a full workshop need distinct handling.
items.try: Write three response examples and the corresponding interface treatment.
items.check: A success shows the reservation. Invalid input focuses the relevant field. A capacity conflict explains what happened and leaves the person able to browse other times.
items.q: No seats are left. The server answers…
a: 409 Conflict, and the screen offers other dates
items.ok: Yes. The conflict is said, and the person keeps a way out.

items.d: According to the PostgreSQL documentation, a transaction bundles multiple steps into a single, all-or-nothing operation. Concurrent requests still need a rule: SELECT … FOR UPDATE locks the workshop’s row, and other transactions that want it wait until the first one ends. That only holds if every write path follows the same rule.

pick.v: BEGIN: the transaction opens. Its changes stay invisible to others until it commits.
SELECT … FOR UPDATE on the workshop’s row: the second request waits here.
Read the remaining seats again, now that nobody else can change them.
INSERT then COMMIT, or ROLLBACK: the booking exists in full, or not at all.

items.ex: Two people request the final seat. Both requests reach the API. One locks the workshop, confirms capacity and commits. The second checks capacity after it acquires the lock.
items.try: Write a test that sends two booking requests for one remaining seat. Run it against a local database.
items.check: Exactly one new booking commits; the other request returns a capacity conflict. Repeating a completed request with the same idempotency key follows the documented replay behaviour.
items.q: Two people ask for the last seat at the same moment. With the row lock…
a: only one goes through; the other gets a capacity conflict
items.ok: Yes. The second waits for the lock, reads again, and finds the workshop full.

items.d: Authentication establishes identity. Authorization checks whether that identity can perform the current operation on the specific resource. Our rule: that check runs on the server, on every request.

pick.v: Sees the public workshops. Sees no bookings.
Sees public data and their own bookings, not anyone else’s.
Edits their own workshops, not another organizer’s.

items.ex: A signed-in organizer can edit their own workshop. A participant only sees their own booking details and public event data.
items.try: Make a permission matrix for anonymous visitors, participants and organizers. Turn each cell into a test case.
items.check: Include an organizer trying to edit a different organizer’s event. A valid session alone does not grant permission for that record.
items.q: A signed-in organizer tries to edit someone else’s workshop. The server…
a: declines: their session gives them no right on that workshop
items.ok: Yes. Being signed in says who you are, not what you may do.

items.h: Ship a release you can diagnose.
items.d: A release needs a known configuration, a repeatable build, a smoke test and a rollback plan. Logs should help explain requests without collecting secrets or unnecessary private data. That is our workshop’s list.

pick.v: Run the checks: nothing ships if one fails.
The smoke test: the workshop list and one test booking.
Release a known version, by its commit identifier.
Verify, and roll back if needed, following each failure by its request ID.

items.ex: Deploy the booking flow to staging. Check the event list and one test booking, validate database changes and correlate failures by request ID.
items.try: Write a pre-release checklist and demonstrate a rollback on a disposable staging deployment.
items.check: Record the working build, expected migration state and smoke-test results. Confirm the previous build remains compatible with the database or prepare a tested recovery plan.
items.q: Before releasing, what do you keep at hand?
a: nothing: we will fix it live
the working build, the expected database state and a tested rollback
items.ok: Yes. A version you can put back beats a fix made live.

w3.lead: For builders: prototype a verifiable attendance receipt on a development network (ethereum.org: a chain designed for local development), with synthetic data. This is education, not an offer.
w3.tabs: The six lessons of the local chain

items.d: A public chain can let independent parties inspect a shared record. It also adds visibility, cost and operational complexity. Our workshop rule: ordinary application data stays in the database, and only the minimum to verify goes on the chain.

pick.v: Bookings and contacts: names, email addresses, guest lists.
A public receipt identifier, nothing personal.
Reads the proof and its status, writes nothing.

items.ex: Attendance receipts could be independently verified. Names, email addresses, guest lists and support notes stay in the booking system.
items.try: List the data you need for a proof. Remove anything that could identify a person without their consent.
items.check: Only the minimum public reference goes on the chain. No email address, and nothing guessed from one.
items.q: What goes on the chain for an attendance receipt?
a: a public receipt identifier, nothing personal
items.ok: Yes. The minimum to verify; the rest stays in the database.

items.h: Read what the wallet is asking.
items.d: A wallet helps people manage signing; a signature authorizes a specific payload under an account key. Connecting, signing a message and signing a transaction are three different actions; ethereum.org calls a transaction a cryptographically signed instruction from an account.

pick.v: The site reads the public address chosen: ethereum.org says it is like a login you can use across many apps.
The screen shows the intended action and the network, before any request.
The person approves this request, and nothing else.
The site checks the result and the network used.

items.ex: The receipt demo reads a wallet address for a local exercise. It requests a write only when the learner explicitly chooses to issue a demo receipt.
items.try: Sketch separate screens for connection, review, approval and cancellation. Use a fresh development wallet, on the local chain.
items.check: The review shows the intended action and network. A declined request leaves the interface usable. The app never asks for a recovery phrase or a private key.
items.q: An app asks for your recovery phrase to “verify” your wallet. That is…
a: a warning sign: never give it
items.ok: Yes. Whoever has the phrase has the wallet: give it to no one.

items.h: Show the difference between a read and a submission.
items.d: ethereum.org’s JSON-RPC documentation: a read (eth_call) runs without creating a transaction on the chain. A write follows a transaction’s life: sending returns its identifier (the hash), and the receipt, which says success or failure, is not available while the transaction is pending. Follow a receipt, state by state.

do: Read the receipt and the state
chain: A receipt with status “success”, under the demo’s rule
lab.src: ethereum.org, JSON-RPC API: the receipt is not available for pending transactions, and its status is 1 (success) or 0 (failure).

items.ex: Read whether a receipt ID exists. When issuing one, show the demo transaction hash and update the status after checking the receipt.
items.try: Design status screens for awaiting approval, submitted, failed and confirmed.
items.check: A hash alone means the action was submitted. The confirmed view relies on a successful receipt and the confirmation rule chosen for the demo.
items.q: Right after sending, the site shows the transaction hash. The operation is…
a: sent, not confirmed yet: it needs the receipt
items.ok: Yes. The hash says “sent”. The receipt says whether it worked.

items.h: Turn the contract into explicit rules.
items.d: A smart contract is code deployed to a network; ethereum.org notes that deployed contract code usually cannot be changed to patch security flaws. Our method: define who may act, what changes and what is announced before wiring a front end, then test the intended and the rejected actions locally.

pick.v: One authorized account issues the demo receipts.
A receipt ID is used only once.
The contract stores the new ID.
A successful issue announces the receipt reference.

items.ex: Only the demo issuer may record a synthetic attendance ID. Duplicate IDs are rejected. A successful issue emits an event.
items.try: Write local tests for issuance, duplicate rejection and an unauthorized account, with synthetic IDs.
items.check: A valid call creates one receipt. Invalid calls create none and leave prior state intact.
items.q: An unauthorized account tries to issue a receipt. The contract…
a: refuses, and the state stays as it was
items.ok: Yes. A refused action leaves no trace in the state.

items.h: Build a useful timeline from events.
items.d: Contract events can feed an application index. Our workshop method: keep the chain and the event’s position with each indexed row, make processing repeatable, and plan for the latest blocks being reorganized, under the chosen chain’s own rule.

pick.v: The contract emits it.
Reads a range of blocks.
Inserts or updates the event’s row.
Shows the indexed state.

items.ex: A receipt page shows a searchable list of demo issuance events. The indexer records the latest processed block and can rebuild the view.
items.try: Replay the same batch twice, then simulate dropping a recent block from the source history.
items.check: The second run creates no duplicates. Rebuilt data matches the history kept after the simulated change.
items.q: The same batch of events is replayed twice. The index…
a: stays the same: one row per event
items.ok: Yes. A repeatable process gives the same index on every run.

items.h: Keep the booking app useful without a wallet.
items.d: Build the normal experience first, then a separate proof-verification path with clear failure states. Our rule: the proof degrades gracefully when the node is down; ethereum.org notes that an app must connect to a node to read the chain.

pick.v: An off-chain record, in the database.
The local-chain demo.
A read-only proof lookup.
The result, and its limits.

items.ex: A workshop organizer issues demo receipts locally. A visitor books without a wallet and can verify an anonymized receipt later.
items.try: Demo the full flow, then disconnect the node. Show the booking flow and the verification state during the outage.
items.check: Booking still works. Verification says the network is unavailable and never claims a proof was checked.
items.q: The node stops answering. The visitor…
a: books anyway; verification says it is unavailable
items.ok: Yes. The proof is an extra; the booking does not depend on it.

all.d: The receipt is stamped. On the client’s side, the Bookshop’s web3 course helps decide whether a chain is needed; we build the ordinary route.

home.name: Home
home.alt: Numidea Labs poster “HOME · YASSER & KURO”: Yasser standing in the workshop among a lamp, books and plans; Kūro on a pile of books, a second cat asleep, a pigeon, a raven and a rat.

home.rule: A project brief can start with one problem, one person, and one result.
home.q: Lantern’s owner asks for “something digital” before the first night class. Where should Yasser start?
a: Ask where a customer gets stuck.
List every feature a competitor has.
f: A logo might help. First find out whether the friction is recognition, information, or the way an order gets handled.
Start with a recent example and an outcome you can observe. The right tool comes after that.
A feature list skips the person who needs to use it. Ask about a real visit or order first.

ex.brief: Match the visitor’s task, their difficulty and the result we want to observe.
choices: Check the session date and price
A visitor must message to confirm a seat
ex.empty: Fill all three parts. A useful brief names the task, where it gets hard, and how you’ll know it improved.
ex.ok: A visitor needs the date and price, but must message to confirm a seat. We’ll test whether they can book straight from the event page.
ex.bad: Match the event you can observe at the end to the result. The friction is what interrupts the task today.

fields.name: Fields
fields.alt: Poster “FIELDS · YASSER & THE CREW”: Yasser in a field of tall grass, a raven on his shoulder, a pigeon in flight; at his feet Kūro, another cat and a rat among books and maps.
fields.lore: Pigeon takes the brief to Lantern and watches two people try to join the night class. Their routes differ. Both stop before choosing a seat.
fields.rule: Discovery turns a guess into a testable observation.
fields.q: You suspect visitors leave because the class date or price is hard to find. What can you collect first?
a: Count how many colors are on the homepage.
Rewrite the event page before watching anyone.
Watch two people try to find the class date and price.
f: Color is easy to count, but it won’t tell you if someone found the session details.
A rewrite could bury the same information again. Find where the user expects it first.
Observe where they look and what they ask. This gives you a concrete place to investigate.
fields.scene: Two routes to the same stall
fields.handoff: Carry the brief into two observed visits.
fields.decision: Field evidence: put the class date and price beside the booking action.

ex.brief: Watch two customers before deciding what needs to move.
ex.obsPhone: Phone visitor opens the class page, scrolls past the poster, and looks for the date in the footer.
ex.obsDesk: Desktop visitor finds the date but opens a message window to ask for the price and seat availability.
ex.one: One observation helps you form a question. Watch the other visit before making a decision.
ex.ok: Both visitors wanted class details before committing. Test putting the date and price beside Book.

audience.rule: A path works when the people who need it can complete it.
audience.q: Lantern’s new form works with a mouse. A keyboard user can’t tell where they are. What changes?
a: Add visible focus and walk the form with Tab.
Make the submit button larger only.
f: Check every field, action and error message in order. You can observe exactly where the journey breaks.
It won’t tell them which control has focus.
Size helps some users. They still need a visible focus state throughout the form.
audience.handoff: Use the new event layout and test it from the first control to Book.
audience.decision: Access check: visible focus follows the booking order through the entire form.

ex.brief: Follow the booking form one control at a time and see why focus visibility matters.
ex.enabled: Focus is now visible. Step through the controls to check their order.
ex.hidden: Focus moved, but the visitor cannot see which control is active. Enable a visible indicator.

identity.rule: Make the identity usable across surfaces with a consistent family of marks.
identity.q: The sign reads well, but the logo turns into a blob in a tiny browser tab. Which asset belongs there?
a: The full wordmark and the tagline.
A compact mark with the same outer shape.
f: The details compete at small size. Keep them for placements with enough space.
It might read, but it loses the connection to the identity the visitor already recognises.
A deliberate small version keeps the strongest cues and drops detail that cannot survive at that size.

architecture.name: Architecture
architecture.alt: Poster “ARCHITECTURE”: Yasser leaning on a giant pencil in the middle of a maze (“backend”, “logic”, “automation”, “structure”); a raven, a pigeon, Kūro and a rat.
architecture.lore: Ratman follows the booking form’s copper line to the relay. The page is ready to take bookings. The relay still has to decide who gets the last seat.
architecture.rule: The server must handle contention for a limited resource before it confirms a booking.
architecture.q: Two customers request the last seat at the same time. Which system should decide who gets it?
a: Confirm both and send a correction later.
The server checks and updates capacity as one protected operation.
Each browser checks its copy of the seat count.
f: That pushes a preventable conflict onto the customers.
Only one request should complete the reservation. The other receives a clear “full” response.
Both browsers might have the same stale count. The decision needs one authoritative write path.

architecture.decision: Relay rule: check and reserve the last seat in one protected server operation.

ex.brief: Run the same two requests through competing capacity rules. See what each visitor gets.
ex.bothMsg: Oversold. Both browsers saw the same old seat count and issued a confirmation.
ex.oneMsg: Exactly one seat was booked. A single protected operation checks capacity and records the booking before confirmation.
ex.more: Run the other rule too, to compare.

launch.rule: Test a release and keep a known recovery path.
launch.q: Lantern is about to publish its new booking flow. What is the best final rehearsal?
a: Place a test booking on staging and confirm the rollback plan.
Open the event page and stop when it loads.
Release and wait for customer messages.
f: Check the meaningful task end to end and know what you will restore if the new release fails.
Loading is useful. It doesn’t tell you if a visitor can reserve a seat and see a confirmation.
Run the core journey yourself while the recovery path is still easy to use.
launch.handoff: Carry the working relay into staging and test the complete booking.
launch.decision: Release decision: keep the working build live until the staging confirmation passes.

ex.brief: Make a staging booking, then decide what to do about the failing release.
ex.r0: Live: previous release · Staging: new release
ex.r1: Staging: booking confirmation fails · Live: previous release
ex.stageMsg: The homepage loads, but the booking fails at confirmation. The exercise begins with the previous release still available.
ex.promoteMsg: Customers now reach a broken order flow. Restore the last working release.
ex.keepB: Keep or restore last working release
ex.keepEarly: You protected the live path. Run a staging booking to see what would have failed.
ex.ok: Live bookings work while you repair the staging build. Re-run the full booking before promoting it.

growth.name: Growth
growth.alt: Poster “GROWTH”: Yasser surrounded by cards (“SEO”, “ANALYTICS”, “CONTENT”, “OPTIMIZATION”) and the crew legend in hand lettering (“KURO”, “RAVEN”, “PIGEON”, “RAT”); all four at the foot of the plinth.
growth.lore: Lantern opens the booking page after the confirmation fix. Raven watches 100 fictional visits. Only 40 people reach the form, which brings Pigeon’s field notes back into focus.
growth.rule: Choose a signal that reflects the task you are improving.
growth.q: More people visit the booking page, but completed bookings barely change. What do you compare?
a: Visits to the page versus completed bookings.
The total likes on the launch post.
The number of posts you wrote.
f: Compare the share that finishes, then inspect the biggest drop-off step before changing it.
Attention can grow without the booking journey improving.
That describes your output, not whether visitors could book.
growth.handoff: After the confirmation fix, compare the live booking stages.
growth.decision: Growth lead: 60 of 100 visits stopped before the form. Test whether the date, price, and booking action are clear.

ex.brief: Inspect a fictional booking funnel. Which step loses the most people?
rows: Visitors
Started booking
Booked
tips: Every person who reached the page.
60 of 100 did not start. Check whether the offer and the next action are clear.
8 of 40 did not complete. That’s a smaller loss than the 60 visitors lost before the form.

observer.name: Observer
observer.alt: Poster “01 / THE OBSERVER · THE NEUTRAL EYE”: a large open eye in the night sky, above a figure in a red coat on a hill.
observer.lore: After the class, a visitor asks for a receipt that someone else can verify. Raven opens a window in the Observatory. The attendee list stays in Lantern’s locked drawer.
observer.rule: Separate public verification from private customer records. This simulation uses fictional receipts.
observer.q: A visitor wants to verify an attendance receipt publicly. What belongs in that record?
a: A crowd photo and the whole list of attendees.
f: That publishes much more than the verifier needs.
Those details are unnecessary for this proof and can reveal private information.
The public lookup can answer whether the demo issuer recorded the receipt. Contact details stay in the booking system.
observer.scene: A window and a locked drawer
observer.handoff: Create an optional receipt lookup after attendance.
observer.decision: Proof boundary: publish only an opaque receipt reference. Keep attendee details private.

ex.brief: Choose which fields the fictional public archive can see. Run a receipt lookup with your choices.
ex.pickMsg: Select what should be visible, then run the lookup.
ex.none: Lookup can’t work without a public receipt reference.
ex.ok: Receipt found. The verifier can check the reference while customer details stay private.
ex.over: The archive would expose details it doesn’t need. Keep only the opaque receipt ID public.

wire.name: Moonlit Wire
wire.alt: MERCURY poster: the traveller in a red coat walks a power line under the full moon, Kūro follows on the wire, the town and its arches below.
wire.lore: Kūro follows Raven out into MERCURY. The crossing is a rehearsal for Lantern’s new receipt screen. Each stepping point offers one action and one visible result.
wire.rule: A complex flow becomes easier when the next safe step is clear.
wire.q: A visitor opens Lantern’s receipt screen for the first time. What should it make easy?
a: Complete one real task and see a clear result.
f: A visual choice can wait until the visitor understands the task.
Give the visitor a short successful path. They can discover advanced controls after they know what the tool does.
That gives a beginner more decisions without a reason to make them.
wire.handoff: Rehearse the receipt screen with Kūro, one meaningful step at a time.
wire.decision: Wayfinding rule: one clear action, followed by a result the visitor can see.

ex.brief: Advance Kūro by giving him a clear next step. There is no timer.
msgs: One clear action at a time.
A visible result tells you what just happened.
Kūro crossed. A short path with visible feedback helps visitors know how to proceed.
ex.jumpMsg: Kūro stays put. The next step is unclear, and a settings detour doesn’t show how the tool works.

ash.name: Ash Field
ash.alt: Poster “04 / MERCURY · WANDER”: the traveller in a red coat walks through a field of dry grass.
ash.lore: The Observatory signal drops beyond the wire. Yasser returns across the ash field with one rule for Lantern: a failed proof lookup must never close the booking desk.
ash.rule: A lost connection should preserve the work the visitor can still do.
ash.q: The proof service goes offline while the booking system remains up. What should the site do?
a: Keep bookings open and show that proof lookup is unavailable.
f: A status the system cannot verify should not be shown as verified.
An optional dependency should not automatically stop an independent task.
Separate flows keep the useful part of the experience available. Say exactly what could not be checked.
ash.handoff: Cut the Observatory connection and see if Lantern can still take bookings.
ash.decision: Outage rule: keep bookings available and say when receipt verification is unavailable.

ex.brief: Disconnect one service and check which parts of the experience still work.
ex.cutMsg: Raven lost the proof signal. The booking path still has its own working connection.
ex.okMsg: Booking succeeded. The receipt could not be verified while the proof service was offline.
ex.normal: Booking succeeds in normal conditions. Now disconnect proof and test again.
ex.plugMsg: Verification is available again. Ask for a new lookup before showing a result.

marque.kind: CLIENT COURSE · YOUR BRAND, BEFORE THE LOGO

marque.desc: Nine districts to prepare your brand before you pay a designer: audience, promise, character, files, name, and a brief for the Studio.
marque.conclusion: Nadia’s brief is complete; yours is too, box by box.

plate.a1: A pastry shop on a street corner at night: a lit window of cakes on stands, a striped awning, a cream signboard still blank, a small table with an open sketchbook.
plate.a2: A print shop: a roller press unrolls a large blank cream banner across the floor, stacks of paper, colour swatch fans, a light table with a blank sheet, rolled posters in a basket.

b1.rule: A logo is a sign: the brand, the identity and their rules are decided before it.
b1.handoff: Nadia knows what she has: a logo, nothing else. Now: who is she remaking it for?
b1.decision: A logo alone is a sign; the rest is decided first.

b2.rule: A design route is judged against the person in the brief, not by taste.
b2.handoff: Her customer has a face; now she needs a promise that customer can check.
b2.decision: Pick the route that speaks to the person in my brief.

b3.rule: A promise counts if a customer can check it: a deadline, a fact, a proof.
b3.handoff: The promise holds; now to tell the designer what people should feel.
b3.decision: A promise that can be checked, with its proof.

b4.rule: Tell the designer the goal, what people should feel; the designer chooses the means.
b4.handoff: The character is said; Nadia now tries her logo in a browser tab.
b4.decision: Say what people should feel, not the colour or the typeface.

b9.rule: A brand is a family: the small version is drawn, not shrunk.
b9.handoff: The logo will be remade, with a compact version; the printer already wants the file for the banner.
b9.decision: A compact version in solid shapes, seen at 16 pixels.

b5.rule: To print large you need the vector file: it stays sharp at every size.
b5.handoff: She knows which files to ask for; a proposal arrives, “all included”.
b5.decision: Ask for the vector file (SVG or PDF) and the versions.

b6.rule: “All included” can only be checked against a written list of what is delivered.
b6.handoff: The proposal is read; the name is left, and who owns it.
b6.decision: Ask in writing for the list of what is delivered.

b7.rule: A paid-for logo is not a registered trademark: registration is separate, country by country.
b7.handoff: The name has its country of registration; now everything comes together on the brief.
b7.decision: Register the name with INAPI for Algeria.

b8.rule: Before the first call: the brief filled in, and one person who decides.
b8.handoff: Nadia’s brief is ready to go, whenever she wants.
b8.decision: Keep the brief at hand, and one person who decides.

argent.pitch: Getting paid from abroad, reading the fees, setting a rate, keeping enough cash, guarding your keys: the money side of remote work, district by district.
argent.search: Earning from far away · Lantern Bookshop | Numidea Labs
argent.desc: Getting paid from abroad, comparing fees, setting your rate, keeping cash in hand and guarding your keys: a free atlas, not financial advice.
argent.conclusion: Selma knows which way the money comes, what it costs her, what to charge and how much to keep aside.

plate.a1: A post-office arcade at dusk: a long wooden counter with sealed envelopes and string-tied parcels, a brass letter scale, empty pigeon lofts on the roof.
plate.a2: A counting room at night: a wooden desk with closed ledgers and an open notebook of blank lines, a small iron strongbox, a calendar of empty squares, a lit lantern and the towers through the window.

argent.toComptoir: To talk it through one to one, the fixed-price services are at the Bookshop’s counter.

pay.name: Route
pay.lore: Selma is an illustrator in Bordj Bou Arréridj; in the evenings she teaches the Lantern’s printmaking class. A publisher abroad wants to pay her for her illustrations. She does not yet know which way the money will travel.
pay.rule: Before the price, the route: which way the money comes in, and what that passage costs.

f.0: The rate matters, but it comes later. First the route: how your bank or the service receives the money, and at what cost.
f.1: Yes. The route first, the price after.
f.2: The invoice matters for a transfer, not its colour. Look at the route: the delay, the fees, and what your bank accepts.

pay.handoff: The publisher is waiting for an answer: bank transfer, platform, marketplace or crypto?
pay.decision: The route first, the price second.

bank.name: Exchange
bank.lore: To receive the publisher’s money, two services show her “0 fees”. Selma distrusts a zero that round.
bank.rule: A “0 fees” is checked in three places: the exchange, the transfer, the card and the withdrawal.

f.0: Yes. A rate worse than the market is a fee that does not say its name.
f.1: The logo says nothing about the price. The cost hides in the exchange rate applied: compare it with the market rate on the same day.
f.2: The follower count says nothing about what you pay. Look at the rate applied: its gap with the market is the real price.

bank.handoff: The service chosen, what to charge per day is still open.
bank.decision: Compare the rate applied, not the poster.

rate.name: Rate
rate.lore: The publisher asks for a day rate. Selma starts from the calculator’s figures before putting in her own.
rate.rule: A rate is worked out: what you want to keep, plus your costs, divided by the days actually billed.

f.0: Not all 22: some days go to prospecting, quotes, admin and time off. Divide by the days billed.
f.1: Yes. Divide by the days billed, not the days worked.
f.2: You cannot bill more days than you work. Fewer are left: prospecting, quotes and time off take their share.

rate.handoff: The rate set, the publisher says he pays at 60 days.
rate.decision: Divide by the days billed, not the days worked.

treso.name: Cash
treso.lore: The publisher pays at 60 days. Selma checks how many months she can last if nothing comes in until then.
treso.rule: Cash in hand is the number of months you last if nothing comes in as planned.

f.0: He will pay, but in two months. Until then you have to last: the client’s delay becomes your cash need.
f.1: Yes. The client’s payment delay becomes your need for cash.
f.2: One more expense eats into your cash cushion. Before saying yes, keep enough to last at least those two months.

treso.handoff: The books in order, a message from “support” lands in her inbox.
treso.decision: The client’s delay becomes my cash need.

crypto.name: Keys
crypto.lore: A message signed “support” arrives, looking official. It mentions the wallet Selma opened to have a look.
crypto.rule: In crypto, what you own is the key: the recovery phrase is given to no one.

f.0: No genuine support ever asks for it. Whoever reads your recovery phrase takes everything: it is a scam.
f.1: Yes. No support asks for it. Ever.
f.2: Not whole, not in pieces: the phrase recreates your keys, and no support asks for it. Ever.

crypto.handoff: Selma keeps her phrase to herself, and her books in order.
crypto.decision: My recovery phrase goes to no one.

route.caseLabel: Selma on the road · an invented example
route.search: The road book · Lantern Bookshop | Numidea Labs
route.desc: Finding clients, pricing, living with time zones, protecting your files and preparing to leave: a free atlas for working from anywhere.
route.conclusion: Selma comes home with her books kept and a full passport.

plate.r1: A rooftop café terrace at dusk: a small table with an open notebook of blank pages, a phone and a glass of tea, string lights, the sea and white houses below.
plate.r2: A railway station hall at night: two round clocks without numerals showing different times, a bench, a luggage trolley with a backpack, a wall socket with its cable, tall arched windows.
plate.r3: A guesthouse room at dawn: an arched window onto the sea, a closed booklet and a plant on the ledge, a calendar of empty squares on the wall, a packed backpack by the door.

route.toKit: The Nomad kit and the fixed-price services are at the Bookshop’s counter.

n1.lore: Selma leaves Bordj for a season and takes her work along. To pay for the road she needs three clients a month; she starts by writing to people.
n1.rule: Clients can be counted: the ones you want, divided by the share who reply, then by the share who sign.

f.0: Yes. One signature per 40 messages, so 120 messages for 3 clients. Or a better message, or a better offer: both rates can be worked on.
f.1: Cutting prices does not make more people reply. Count: one signature per 40 messages, so 120 messages for 3 clients, or a better rate.
f.2: Waiting does not fill the month. Clients answer messages: at this pace, 120 for 3 signatures, or a better message.

n1.handoff: A first client replies: he wants a price.
n1.decision: One signature per 40 messages: aim for 120, or write better.

n2.lore: The first client wants a figure that will not move. Selma counts her days before she answers.
n2.rule: A project price: the day rate, times the days estimated, plus a margin for the unforeseen.

f.0: If the price was fixed and the scope unchanged, the overrun is not the client’s: that is what the margin is for.
f.1: Yes, if the price was firm. It is the Studio’s rule: “if the work overruns, the difference is on us”. If the scope changes, that is a new quote.
f.2: Splitting the overrun goes back on a fixed price. With the same scope, the margin pays for the unforeseen.

n2.handoff: The price accepted, it still has to go in the quote.
n2.decision: The margin pays for the unforeseen; the fixed price does not move.

n3.lore: Before starting, Selma writes her quote: what is included, and what is not.
n3.rule: A signed quote answers the awkward questions in advance: the scope, the deposit, the revisions, the ownership, the deadline.

f.0: Not that one: at the Studio, two rounds per stage are included. The third is priced separately.
f.1: Yes. Two rounds per stage are included; further ones are quoted separately.
f.2: It is not refused: the Studio’s quote prices it separately, beyond the two rounds included per stage.

n3.handoff: The quote signed, the kick-off call has to fit a client six time zones further west.
n3.decision: Two rounds per stage, the rest priced apart: it is in the quote.

n4.lore: Selma is at UTC+1, her client at UTC−5. She looks for the hour where their two days meet.
n4.rule: Calls go in the hours the two days share; the rest is done in writing.

f.0: At 10:00 your time it is 4:00 for your client: his day has not begun. Look for the hours your two days share.
f.1: Yes. 16:00 for you is 10:00 for your client: the hour falls inside both days.
f.2: At 23:00 your time, your day is over. Put the call in the shared hours: 16:00 for you, 10:00 for him.

n4.handoff: The call set, Selma takes the train again, the laptop and the drive in the same bag.

n5.lore: On the night train her whole office fits in one bag: the laptop, the backup drive, the cables.
n5.rule: Three copies, on two devices, one of them kept outside the bag.

f.0: A password guards access, not the files that left with the bag. What was missing was a copy kept elsewhere.
f.1: Yes. That is the “1” in 3-2-1: one copy outside the bag, online or with someone you trust.
f.2: A second laptop in the same bag would go with the first. What was missing was a copy outside the bag.

n5.handoff: The copies safe, Selma has to log in at the airport.
n5.decision: Three copies, two devices, one elsewhere.

n6.lore: At the airport, Selma has to open her work email before boarding.
n6.rule: On the road your accounts are worth more than your kit: a network you control, two-step verification, one password per account.

f.0: ANSSI and the NCSC both advise avoiding networks you do not control. Go through your phone’s mobile network.
f.1: Yes. The mobile network rather than a network you do not control: that is the NCSC’s advice, and ANSSI’s.
f.2: A public computer is no more yours than public Wi-Fi. The safest is still your phone’s hotspot.

n6.handoff: Landed, Selma adds up her week.
n6.decision: The phone’s network rather than public Wi-Fi.

n7.lore: On the guesthouse terrace, Selma counts her days: five worked, but how many billed?
n7.rule: A year has 52 weeks, but you bill only part of them: count your billed days before promising yourself an income.

f.0: Not all five: prospecting, quotes, admin and learning take days too. At 60%, that makes 3 billed days.
f.1: Yes. The other two days are real: prospecting, quotes, paperwork, learning. Your day rate is what pays for them.
f.2: Fewer than five, but not that few: 60% of 5 days is 3 billed days.

n7.handoff: The season ends; before the next trip, the days of stay are still to be counted.
n7.decision: My rate also pays for the days not billed.

n8.lore: For the next season, Selma plans the Schengen area, with one day out in the middle.
n8.rule: Before the ticket, four files: the stay, taxes, health, the bank. The questions here, the answers from those who give them.

f.0: One day out erases nothing: you count 180 days back from each day of the stay.
f.1: Yes. You count back 180 days from each day of your stay: leaving for a day erases nothing. The Commission’s calculator does the count for you.
f.2: The counter does not pause: it looks at the 180 days before, on each day of the stay.

n8.handoff: The book is full: Selma heads home to Bordj.
n8.decision: Count over 180 days, with the Commission’s calculator.

jeu.caseLabel: The Lantern’s card · an invented example
jeu.search: Fair play · Lantern Bookshop | Numidea Labs
jeu.desc: Gamification without the smoke: what it is, what research says, what it brings, when it harms, and this site’s own rules. A free atlas.
jeu.conclusion: The Lantern has its card: eight boxes, a voice, a drawing at the end. Nothing forces it.

act.j3: Act III · The price and the limit

plate.j1: A small arcade at night: two game cabinets with dark screens under a striped awning, a shelf of soft toys, a checkerboard floor, warm lantern light.
plate.j2: A corner of the Bookshop’s stall: a cork board of cream loyalty cards, a rubber stamp and an inkpad, a small trophy cup, a sheet of star stickers, under the striped awning.
plate.j3: A reading room at night: one armchair under a lamp, a closed handheld console on a shelf among books, an abstract framed print on the wall, a doorway open onto the towers.

g1.name: Level 1
g1.lore: The Lantern’s bookseller wants the night-class students to come back. Before talking loyalty cards, she looks up what gamification means.
g1.rule: Gamification lends a game’s spring to an activity that stays the real thing.

f.0: A whole game is a game, not gamification: gamification borrows a game’s spring for an activity that is not one.
f.1: Yes. The course is still a course; the bar lends it one of a game’s springs: seeing that you are moving forward.
f.2: A mascot alone is decoration. If you take the game away and nothing useful remains, it was not gamification.

g1.handoff: A loyalty card, then? Which need it would feed is still open.
g1.decision: The class stays a class; it borrows one spring from games.

g2.name: Level 2
g2.lore: The card would show the sessions already attended. The bookseller wonders what that is for.
g2.rule: A good game feeds three needs: feeling capable, free, connected.

f.0: Yes: it shows the road already covered. It is competence made visible.
f.1: Freedom is choosing your path and your pace. A progress bar mostly shows the way already done: that is competence.
f.2: Connection is playing with others. A progress bar shows what you have already done: it feeds the need to feel capable.

g2.handoff: The need found, the bookseller wants to know whether it really works.
g2.decision: The card shows the way done: it serves competence.

g3.name: Level 3
g3.lore: Before paying the printer, the bookseller reads what the studies say.
g3.rule: Real, modest effects that depend on context: nothing more to promise.

f.0: The studies find small but real effects, not all equally solid, and dependent on context. No serious person promises “every time”.
f.1: Yes: real, modest effects that depend on the context. Nobody serious promises more.
f.2: The studies do find effects, small but real, when gamification is designed for its audience.

g3.handoff: Cautious, she moves on to the mechanics, one by one.
g3.decision: Real, modest effects: promise nothing more.

g4.name: Level 4
g4.lore: The printer offers two card designs for the same number of sessions. The bookseller hesitates.
g4.rule: You pick one or two mechanics for a purpose, not ten for decoration.

f.0: The same effort, but nothing has started. The ten-box card with two already stamped is finished more often: that is endowed progress.
f.1: Yes. The same effort, but you have already started: that is the endowed progress effect.
f.2: Nunes and Drèze found a difference: the card that starts at 2 of 10 is finished more often, and faster.

g4.handoff: The card drawn, what it says about the Lantern remains.
g4.decision: A card that starts with two boxes stamped.

g5.name: Level 5
g5.lore: A card is also a voice. The bookseller wonders what hers will say about the Lantern.
g5.rule: Play gives a brand a voice, a world and a reason to come back; it serves the message, it does not replace it.

f.0: This level is a practitioners’ reading: what a brand gains first is a character people recognise, not data.
f.1: Yes. The rest may follow, but character is what brings people back.
f.2: Clicks may follow, but what brings people back is character: a voice, a world, a ritual.

g5.handoff: Before launching her card, the bookseller looks at real cases.
g5.decision: The Lantern keeps its voice: that is what brings people back.

g6.name: Level 6
g6.lore: Someone quotes impressive figures to the bookseller. She asks where they come from.
g6.rule: Read where a figure comes from: a published study, a company, or a brand campaign.

f.0: Starbucks’s figure comes from the company itself: useful, to be read as such. The scientific paper is Foldit.
f.1: Yes. The others are company or campaign figures: useful, and to be read as such.
f.2: The speed camera lottery is a famous but fragile case, from a campaign. The scientific paper is Foldit.

g6.handoff: The figures read, the bookseller looks for where it breaks.
g6.decision: Read where a figure comes from before believing it.

g7.name: Level 7
g7.lore: The bookseller was thinking of promising a discount at the end of the card. First she checks what makes such projects fail.
g7.rule: Play can demotivate, push, trap: most failures come from the design.

f.0: Gartner does not say people dislike playing: it forecast failures mostly because of poor design.
f.1: Yes. It is not the game that fails, it is the game badly thought out for its goal.
f.2: Gartner does not point at the technology; it points at poor design.

g7.handoff: The rules of her card are still to be written.
g7.decision: No pressure, no reward promised in advance.

g8.name: Level 8
g8.lore: The bookseller writes her card’s rules by looking at how this site plays.
g8.rule: Nothing starts by itself, the price does not play, a drawing rather than a discount, nothing leaves here, no pressure.

f.0: No discount here: seven seals open a drawing. No reward is traded for a purchase.
f.1: Yes. That is our rule: we reward with something to look at, never with pressure to buy.
f.2: There is no account and no ranking: the seals stay in your browser, and they open a drawing.

g8.decision: The Lantern’s card gives a print from the class, never a discount.

web3.pitch: You were sold a chain; perhaps all you wanted was loyal customers. Eight steps to tell the tool from the result, and leave with a brief that can be priced. Sometimes a chain is the right tool; this course helps you tell when. This is education: no investment advice, no signals, no promise of gain.
web3.search: Web3, without the smoke · Lantern Bookshop | Numidea Labs
web3.desc: Eight districts to find out whether you need a blockchain before you pay: the words, the six-question tree, costs, scams, the law, a brief.
web3.conclusion: Samia keeps the ordinary route; your brief says which is yours.

plate.a1: A small women’s gym at closing time, empty: lockers, rolled mats, a reception counter with a board of stamped loyalty cards and, set apart at the end of the counter, a small glowing teal cube.
plate.a2: A records room: a card-index cabinet with an open drawer and, on the workbench beside it, a chain of small cream blocks linked by brass rings, the only thing glowing teal, among a ruler, a screwdriver and a stapler.
plate.a3: A narrow alley at night: a stall under a too-bright blank banner, a fishing hook hanging on a line above it, wisps of smoke; at the far end, a closed arched wooden gate under a brass lamp.

w1.rule: Signing means agreeing: you do not sign what you do not understand.
w1.handoff: Samia has written her idea without jargon; now: does she need a chain?
w1.decision: Do not sign until I know what it authorises.

w2.rule: If only one party writes to the register, a database is enough.
w2.handoff: No chain; now to say what she really wants.

w3.rule: Start from the result you want, then take the simplest route that gets there.
w3.handoff: The route is chosen; now to see what would go on a chain, and what stays with her.
w3.decision: Points in a database, not a token.

w8.rule: The hash says “sent”; only the receipt says whether it worked.
w8.handoff: Her members’ data stays in her database; now to count what is paid for afterwards.
w8.decision: Wait for the receipt, not just the hash.
w8.foldNote: exercise folded: your route is the ordinary one, with no chain

w4.rule: A complete proposal also shows what is paid for after launch.
w4.handoff: The after-launch lines are noted; the supplier comes back by private message.
w4.decision: Ask for the after-launch lines, even without figures.

w5.rule: A completed transaction cannot be called back: urgency and a look-alike link are the signs.
w5.handoff: Samia did not click; the law is left, where her members are.
w5.decision: Do not click: a completed transaction does not come back.

w6.rule: The law that counts is the law where your users are: in Dubai, VARA.
w6.handoff: The law card is read; everything comes together on the brief.
w6.decision: For a token in Dubai: a VARA-licensed provider, or its consent.

w7.rule: The law first, the code second.
w7.handoff: Samia’s brief is ready to go, whenever she wants.
